subject: biology
title: Cell junctions and the extracellular matrix
summary: What lies outside the cell membrane, and how neighbouring cells hold together, seal off and talk to each other.

concepts.name: Extracellular matrix
concepts.summary: The network of proteins and sugars that cells make and release outside their membrane, which supports tissues and signals to the cells in them.

elements.name: Made by resident cells and secreted

explain.text: Outside the plasma membrane of an animal cell lies the extracellular matrix, a mesh of fibres and sugar-rich gels. Its main parts are collagen, which gives strength, and proteoglycans, which hold water. Cells that live in a tissue make these parts inside themselves and then release them outward, where they join the mesh. The matrix does more than fill space. It anchors cells, guides them as they move, and stores growth factors that signal them. Cells sense how stiff it is and react. A tendon is a good picture: its fibres are laid down by the fibroblasts that live among them.

misconceptions.claim: The matrix is passive packing that holds cells apart and has no effect on what they do.
misconceptions.correction: The matrix signals to cells. Its stiffness changes how cells move, divide and specialise, and it stores growth factors that switch cells on.

misconceptions.claim: The matrix is made outside the cells, from the blood or the environment.
misconceptions.correction: Resident cells make its components inside themselves and secrete them, so the cells decide what the matrix contains.

misconceptions.claim: Only plant cells have an extracellular matrix, and it is the cell wall.
misconceptions.correction: Animal cells have an extracellular matrix of collagen and proteoglycans and no cell wall. Plants have a matrix too, and their cell wall is part of it.

concepts.name: Cell wall
concepts.summary: The stiff outer wall of plant, fungal and bacterial cells, which resists water pressure and lets the cell grow.

explain.text: A plant cell has a wall outside its plasma membrane, made mainly of cellulose fibres set in a gel of other sugars. The wall is stiff enough to resist the pressure that water builds up inside the cell, which keeps a healthy plant firm rather than bursting. It is not a fixed shell, though. Young walls are loosened and stretched as the cell grows, and some cells then add a thicker secondary wall. Fungi and bacteria also have walls, built from other materials such as chitin and peptidoglycan. Animal cells have no cell wall at all.

misconceptions.claim: Animal cells have a cell wall too, just a thinner one.
misconceptions.correction: Animal cells have no cell wall. They rely on the plasma membrane and the extracellular matrix outside it.

misconceptions.claim: The cell wall keeps water out, which is why plant cells do not burst.
misconceptions.correction: Water still enters by osmosis. The wall pushes back against the pressure that builds up inside, and that stops the cell bursting.

misconceptions.claim: A cell wall is a fixed shell, so it stops the cell growing bigger.
misconceptions.correction: The primary wall is loosened and stretched as the cell takes in water and expands, so the cell can grow.

misconceptions.claim: All cell walls are made of cellulose, like plant walls.
misconceptions.correction: Fungi build walls from chitin and bacteria from peptidoglycan. Cellulose is the main material of plant walls only.

concepts.name: Tight junction
concepts.summary: A belt-like seal that closes the gap between neighbouring epithelial cells and fences the cell membrane into regions.

elements.name: Sealing strands of claudin and occludin

explain.text: A tight junction is a seal between neighbouring epithelial cells, the sheet-like cells that line the gut and other surfaces. Strands of claudin and occludin proteins join the two membranes in a continuous belt around each cell, so the gap between the cells is blocked. Substances must then cross through the cells, where the membrane can control them. The strands also act as a fence, keeping the membrane proteins on the top of the cell apart from those on its sides. Tight junctions are found in animals, and they make the gut and the blood-brain barrier selective.

misconceptions.claim: Tight junctions are pores that let water and ions pass between cells.
misconceptions.correction: Tight junctions seal the gap between cells, so substances cannot slip through it. Pores that join the cells' cytoplasm are gap junctions.

misconceptions.claim: Tight junctions are spot glue that holds cells together against pulling.
misconceptions.correction: Spot anchors that resist pulling are desmosomes. Tight junctions form a continuous seal around each cell.

misconceptions.claim: Membrane proteins drift freely over the whole cell, so tight junctions do not divide the membrane.
misconceptions.correction: Tight junction strands act as a fence. They keep the proteins on the top side of an epithelial cell apart from those on its sides.

concepts.name: Desmosome
concepts.summary: A spot-like anchoring junction that holds neighbouring cells together through keratin filaments, so a pull is shared across a tissue.

explain.text: A desmosome is a spot-like anchoring junction between two cells. Cadherin proteins from each cell stick across the narrow gap between them, and a dense plaque inside each cell holds keratin intermediate filaments. Because the filaments run through the cytoplasm and join neighbouring cells, a pull on one cell is spread across a sheet of tissue. Desmosomes do not seal the gap, and they pass nothing from cell to cell. Skin and heart muscle, which are stretched and squeezed, contain many of them.

misconceptions.claim: Desmosomes seal the gap between cells so nothing can leak through.
misconceptions.correction: Sealing is a tight junction's job. Desmosomes are spots that hold cells together under stress, and the gap stays open.

misconceptions.claim: Desmosomes are channels that let ions and small molecules pass between cells.
misconceptions.correction: The channels that pass ions are gap junctions. A desmosome has no pore between the cells.

misconceptions.claim: A desmosome is only a spot where two membranes fuse, with nothing inside the cell.
misconceptions.correction: Inside each cell a plaque anchors keratin filaments, which spread pulling forces across the tissue.

concepts.name: Gap junction
concepts.summary: A channel that joins two neighbouring cells directly, letting ions and small molecules pass from one cytoplasm to the other.

explain.text: A gap junction is a set of channels that join two neighbouring cells directly. Each channel is built from connexin proteins, and two halves, one in each membrane, line up to form a pore. Ions and small molecules pass through, so the cytoplasm of the two cells becomes one continuous space for them. Gap junctions let electrical signals spread from cell to cell, and heart muscle depends on them to beat as one unit. Large molecules cannot pass, and the channels close when calcium rises or the cell becomes acidic.

misconceptions.claim: Gap junctions let any molecule pass, including large proteins.
misconceptions.correction: The pore is narrow. Ions and small molecules pass, and large molecules such as proteins cannot.

misconceptions.claim: Gap junctions pass signals by releasing chemicals into the space between cells, like a synapse.
misconceptions.correction: A gap junction is a direct channel between two cytoplasms. Nothing is released into the gap.

misconceptions.claim: Gap junctions are always open, so damage or signals spread freely to every neighbour.
misconceptions.correction: Gap junctions close in response to changes such as a rise in calcium or a fall in pH, which isolates damaged cells.

concepts.name: Plasmodesma
concepts.summary: Membrane-lined channels through the cell walls of plants that connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

explain.text: A plasmodesma is a channel that crosses the cell wall between two neighbouring plant cells. The plasma membrane of each cell lines the channel, so the two cells share a continuous cytoplasm. A strand of endoplasmic reticulum runs through the centre. Sugars, small ions and some small signalling molecules move through it. Plasmodesmata are not simply open holes: callose can narrow them, which lets a plant control which signals pass between its cells.

misconceptions.claim: Plasmodesmata are just holes in the cell wall with nothing inside.
misconceptions.correction: Each is lined by the plasma membrane and holds a strand of endoplasmic reticulum, so the cytoplasm of the two cells is continuous.

misconceptions.claim: Plasmodesmata are always wide open, so nothing is regulated between plant cells.
misconceptions.correction: Callose can narrow plasmodesmata and reduce what passes, so plants control movement between their cells.

misconceptions.claim: Plasmodesmata are plant gap junctions and work in exactly the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Both link neighbouring cells, but plasmodesmata cross a cell wall and contain an ER strand, which gap junctions lack.

items.prompt: Which protein is the most abundant in the animal extracellular matrix?
choices: Haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in blood
Actin, which forms filaments inside cells
Collagen, which gives the matrix strength
Insulin, which regulates blood sugar
items.explanation: Collagen is the most abundant protein of the matrix and gives it strength. Haemoglobin carries oxygen, actin is a filament inside cells, and insulin is a hormone, so none of them is a matrix protein.

items.prompt: Where are the components of the extracellular matrix made?
choices: In the blood, which soaks them into the tissue
In the nucleus, which exports the finished matrix
Inside the resident cells, which then secrete them
In the wall of neighbouring cells, which grows outward
items.explanation: Cells that live in a tissue make matrix components inside themselves and secrete them, so the cells decide what the matrix holds. Blood does not supply the matrix, and the nucleus holds the genes rather than exporting finished matrix.

items.prompt: Which molecule binds a cell to the extracellular matrix through its surface?
choices: Aquaporin, which moves water across membranes
Integrin, which spans the membrane and grips matrix
Cellulose, which forms the plant cell wall
Histone, which packs DNA into chromatin
items.explanation: Integrins are membrane-spanning receptors that grip matrix proteins such as fibronectin and laminin, and link the matrix to the cell's inside. Cellulose is a plant wall polymer, aquaporins move water, and histones pack DNA.

items.prompt: Single cells are placed on a surface that gets stiffer from one side to the other. Which way do they tend to move?
choices: Towards the softer side
Towards the stiffer side
They stay put; stiffness has no effect
At random; they cannot sense stiffness
items.explanation: Cells sense how stiff their surroundings are and move towards stiffer areas, a behaviour called durotaxis. A matrix that did nothing would give them no reason to choose a side.

items.prompt: A student says: 'The matrix is just packing between cells, so its make-up does not change how they behave.' Which reply is correct?
choices: The matrix signals cells and changes how they move, grow and specialise
The matrix only holds cells apart, so they never touch one another
The matrix is made of cell walls, which cannot send any signals
The matrix is made of blood, so its make-up is the same everywhere
items.explanation: The matrix is a signalling environment: its stiffness and its stored growth factors change what cells do. It is not a passive gap filler, and animal cells have no wall that could be the matrix.

items.prompt: A wound heals, and new matrix fills the gap within days. Where did that matrix come from?
choices: Blood plasma that leaked into the wound and set
Cells near the wound, which made it and released it
Bacteria that drifted into the wound and spun threads
Skin cells' nuclei, which moved out of the cells
items.explanation: Cells near a wound make matrix components and release them into the gap. Plasma can leak into a wound but does not set into matrix, and bacteria do not build the matrix of animal tissue.

items.prompt: Which statement about the extracellular matrix is correct?
choices: Animal cells have an extracellular matrix but no cell wall
Only plant cells have an extracellular matrix, and it is the wall
Only bacteria have a matrix, and it is made of collagen
Animal and plant matrices always have the same composition
items.explanation: Animal cells make a matrix of collagen, proteoglycans and glycoproteins, and they have no wall. Plant cells have a matrix too, and their wall is part of it. Bacteria do not make collagen, and plant and animal matrices differ in make-up.

items.prompt: Stem cells are grown on a soft gel that mimics brain tissue, then on a stiff gel that mimics bone. Which best explains why they become different cell types?
choices: Matrix stiffness changes which genes the cells switch on
The gels contain different genes that the cells copy directly
Stiffness has no effect; only the nutrients in the gel matter
The cells were grown at different times, so they age differently
items.explanation: Matrix stiffness acts on cells through signals that change which genes are active. Soft, brain-like gels favour neuron-like cells and stiff, bone-like gels favour bone-forming cells. Gels carry no genes for cells to copy.

items.prompt: Which polymer forms the main load-bearing fibres of a plant cell wall?
choices: Glycogen, a storage sugar in animals and fungi
Cellulose, a long chain of glucose units
Keratin, a tough protein in hair and nails
Collagen, a fibrous protein of animal tissue
items.explanation: Cellulose forms long microfibrils that give the plant cell wall its strength. Glycogen is a storage sugar, while keratin and collagen are structural proteins, and none of them is the main fibre of a plant wall.

items.prompt: Which of these cells has a cell wall outside its plasma membrane?
choices: A red blood cell in a human
A nerve cell in a human body
A mature leaf cell in a tree
A skin cell in a human body
items.explanation: A plant cell, such as a leaf cell, has a wall outside its plasma membrane. Animal cells, including red blood cells, nerve cells and skin cells, have no cell wall.

items.prompt: Which molecule is the main building material of a bacterial cell wall?
choices: Cellulose, the same polymer as in plant walls
Peptidoglycan, a mesh of sugars and short peptides
Collagen, the protein of animal matrix
Keratin, the protein of hair and nails
items.explanation: Bacterial walls are built mainly from peptidoglycan, a mesh of sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides. Cellulose is the plant wall material, and collagen and keratin are animal proteins.

items.prompt: A plant cell takes in water until it is firm, but it does not burst. What stops it bursting?
choices: The wall stops any water from entering the cell
The wall pushes back on the pressure built up inside
The membrane shrinks so that it fits within the wall
The wall pumps excess water out through its pores
items.explanation: Water enters the cell by osmosis and builds turgor pressure inside it. The wall is stiff enough to push back on that pressure, so the cell stays firm. The wall does not stop water entering, and the membrane does not shrink to fit it.

items.prompt: A student says: 'A cell wall is a fixed shell, so a plant cell cannot grow bigger.' What is wrong with that?
choices: The wall loosens and stretches as the cell expands
The wall never changes, so cells grow only by dividing
The wall is made of living cells that can pull apart
The wall is removed in the middle of growth and replaced
items.explanation: The primary wall is loosened and stretched while the cell expands, so the cell can grow without splitting. Walls are not living, and they are not removed and rebuilt during normal growth.

items.prompt: Which statement about fungal and bacterial cell walls is correct?
choices: They use other materials, such as chitin or peptidoglycan
They are made of cellulose, the same as plant walls
They are made of collagen, the same as animal matrix
Animal cells have walls too, like those of fungi
items.explanation: Fungi build their walls mainly from chitin and bacteria from peptidoglycan. Cellulose is the plant wall material, collagen is an animal matrix protein, and animal cells have no walls.

items.prompt: A plant cell is placed in a strong salt solution, and its membrane pulls away from the wall. What happens to the wall?
choices: It keeps its size, and only the membrane shrinks
It blocks water loss, so the membrane cannot move
It collapses inward, pulled along with the membrane
It dissolves in the salt solution and disappears
items.explanation: In a strong salt solution water leaves the cell, so the membrane pulls away from the wall while the rigid wall keeps its shape. A wall does not block water loss, and it does not dissolve in salt.

items.prompt: A plant cell takes in a lot of water and grows much larger. What lets the wall allow this?
choices: The primary wall loosens and stretches as the cell expands
The wall is fixed in size, so the cell must divide to grow
The wall is made of cellulose, which stretches like rubber
The wall has no effect, since water enters through the membrane
items.explanation: Primary walls loosen and stretch as the cell takes in water, so the cell can enlarge. The wall is not fixed in size, and cellulose does not stretch like rubber. Water does pass through the membrane, but the wall still has to give way.

items.prompt: Which proteins form the sealing strands of a tight junction?
choices: Cadherins and catenins
Claudins and occludins
Keratin and vimentin
Integrins and fibronectin
items.explanation: Claudins and occludins are transmembrane proteins that form the strands of a tight junction. Cadherins and catenins belong to adhesive junctions, keratin and vimentin are filaments inside cells, and integrins bind the matrix.

items.prompt: Which cells have tight junctions that seal the gap between neighbours?
choices: Red blood cells floating in the blood plasma
Epithelial cells lining the inside of the gut
Bone-forming cells inside the bone marrow
Plant leaf cells, which connect through plasmodesmata
items.explanation: Epithelial cells form sheets that line the gut and other surfaces, and tight junctions seal the gaps between them. Red blood cells and bone-forming cells are not epithelia, and plant cells join through plasmodesmata instead.

items.prompt: What is the main job of a tight junction?
choices: It seals the gap, so substances cannot slip between the cells
It lets ions pass straight from one cell into the next
It holds cells together against strong pulling forces
It stores calcium so that nerve cells can fire
items.explanation: A tight junction is a belt of sealing strands that closes the gap between neighbouring epithelial cells, so substances must cross the cells themselves. Pulling strength comes from desmosomes, and the passage of ions between cells is what a tight junction blocks.

items.prompt: A student says: 'Tight junctions are pores that let water and ions pass between cells.' What is wrong with that?
choices: They seal the gap completely, so nothing slips through it
They are spot anchors that pull cells together under strain
They are gap channels that pass proteins to the neighbours
They are pores that let small molecules pass in both directions
items.explanation: A tight junction is a continuous seal, so the gap is blocked rather than opened. Spot anchors are desmosomes, and channels that pass molecules from cell to cell are gap junctions, which are a different structure.

verification.note: b's note: Some claudins form ion pores; the statement is wrong mainly because junctions seal.

items.prompt: What does a tight junction do to the membrane of an epithelial cell?
choices: It keeps the top and side membranes distinct
It lets membrane proteins drift from the top to the side
It fuses the two cells' membranes into one sheet
It exists only in brain cells, not in the gut
items.explanation: Tight junction strands act as a fence within the membrane. Proteins on the top (apical) side and the side (basolateral) stay in their own regions, which keeps the cell polarised. Membrane proteins do not drift freely from one region to the other.

items.prompt: A drug breaks down the sealing strands in the gut lining. What is the most likely result?
choices: Substances pass between cells that should be blocked
Cells lose their ability to divide and the lining thins
Cells form stronger links that stop nutrients entering
The lining stores extra calcium inside the cells
items.explanation: The sealing strands close the gaps between gut cells. If they fail, molecules that should be kept out of the tissue beneath can leak through between the cells. The other choices name effects that the strands do not control.

items.prompt: A tight junction and a desmosome both join two neighbouring cells. Which pair of jobs is correct?
choices: Tight junctions seal the gap; desmosomes resist pulling
Tight junctions resist pulling; desmosomes seal the gap
Both only let small ions pass through the gap
Both are channels that join the cytoplasm of two cells
items.explanation: Tight junctions are seals that close the gap between cells. Desmosomes are spot anchors that spread pulling forces. The wrong pair gives the tight junction the anchoring job, which belongs to desmosomes.

items.prompt: Brain capillaries are sealed by tight junctions. Why does that help control what reaches brain tissue?
choices: Substances must pass through the cells, where they can be screened
Substances pass freely between cells, so the barrier relies on speed
Tight junctions open to let nutrients in between the cells
Tight junctions glue the blood cells to the brain tissue
items.explanation: Capillaries in the brain have tight junctions, so most substances must cross the endothelial cells themselves, where transporters and membranes can filter them. Junctions do not open to admit nutrients, and they do not stick cells to tissue.

items.prompt: A protein sits only on the top side of an epithelial cell. Why does it not spread to the side membrane?
choices: Tight junctions form a fence that keeps the two regions apart
Membrane proteins drift freely, so it would soon reach the side
The protein is too large to fit into the side membrane
Proteins on the side membrane destroy any protein from the top
items.explanation: Tight junction strands form a fence within the membrane, so proteins on the top (apical) side and the side (basolateral) stay in their own regions. Membrane proteins do not drift freely across the whole cell.

items.prompt: Which proteins link two neighbouring cells across a desmosome?
choices: Connexins, which form the pores
Claudins, which form the seal
Cadherins, which bind across the gap
Integrins, which grip the matrix
items.explanation: Cadherins from each cell bind to each other across the narrow gap of a desmosome. Connexins form gap junction pores, claudins form tight junction seals, and integrins grip the matrix rather than another cell.

items.prompt: What does the inner plaque of a desmosome anchor?
choices: Microtubules, which run through the cytoplasm
Nothing, since the plaque only touches the membrane
Intermediate filaments, such as keratin fibres
Ribosomes, which build the cell's proteins
items.explanation: The inner plaque of a desmosome holds intermediate filaments, mainly keratin in skin. Microtubules, ribosomes and the membrane itself are not what the plaque anchors.

items.prompt: In which tissue are desmosomes especially common, because the tissue is stretched and rubbed?
choices: The outer layer of the skin
The fluid part of the blood
The hard centre of a bone
The inside of a chloroplast
items.explanation: The outer layer of skin is stretched and rubbed, so it is packed with desmosomes that share the load. Blood plasma is a fluid, a bone's centre is not an epithelium, and a chloroplast is an organelle inside a plant cell.

items.prompt: A student says: 'A desmosome has nothing inside the cell, just a bond between two membranes.' What is wrong with that?
choices: Its plaque anchors keratin filaments, which spread the pull
Its plaque is made of collagen, which absorbs water
It has a pore that connects the two cells' cytoplasm
It is only a spot where two membranes fuse together
items.explanation: The inner plaque holds keratin intermediate filaments, which run through the cell and spread a pull across the tissue. A desmosome has no pore, and it is more than a spot where membranes are fused.

items.prompt: A tissue is pulled hard enough to tear. Which cell junction most directly resists the tearing?
choices: Desmosomes, which anchor cells to a filament network
Gap junctions, which pass ions between neighbouring cells
Tight junctions, which seal the gap between neighbouring cells
Nuclear pores, which let mRNA leave the nucleus
items.explanation: Desmosomes are built to take strain: cadherins hold neighbouring cells and keratin filaments carry the load across the tissue. Gap and tight junctions are not built to bear strain, and nuclear pores are not cell junctions.

items.prompt: Which statement about desmosomes is correct?
choices: They hold cells together under stress without sealing the gap
They seal the gap so that nothing can leak between cells
They pass ions from one cell's cytoplasm to the next
They float free in the membrane and never touch the other cell
items.explanation: A desmosome is an anchoring spot, not a seal or a channel. Its cadherins bind across the gap and its filaments spread the load, so the gap stays open.

items.prompt: Skin cells lose their desmosomes. What is the most likely result?
choices: The skin blisters and tears as its cells pull apart
Ions stop passing from one skin cell to the next
Water can no longer enter the skin cells at all
The skin stops making keratin for its filaments
items.explanation: Without desmosomes, skin cells cannot share strain, so under pull they separate and the skin blisters. Desmosomes do not carry ions, and they do not control water entry or keratin production.

items.prompt: Two skin cells are joined by desmosomes whose filaments run into each cell. One cell is pulled. What happens next?
choices: The pull spreads through the filament network to neighbours
The pull is absorbed by the gap and blocked there
The pull travels through a pore into the next cell
The pull stays inside the one cell that was pulled
items.explanation: Desmosomes join the filament networks of neighbouring cells, so force passes from cell to cell and across the sheet. The gap is not a barrier to that force, and no pore carries it.

items.prompt: Hemidesmosomes attach the basal cells of skin to the matrix below. Which description is most accurate?
choices: They link intermediate filaments to matrix proteins through integrins
They link two neighbouring cells together through cadherins
They pass ions from the cell straight into the matrix
They seal the matrix tightly against the surface of the cell
items.explanation: A hemidesmosome anchors intermediate filaments to the matrix through integrins, so the cell is tied to the matrix rather than to a neighbour. It does not pass ions or seal anything, and it is not a cell-to-cell junction.

items.prompt: What are gap junction channels built from?
choices: Cadherin proteins that bind two cells
Claudin proteins that form a seal
Connexin proteins that form pores
Keratin proteins that form filaments
items.explanation: Each gap junction channel is built from connexin proteins. Six connexins form a connexon in each membrane, and two connexons join across the gap. Cadherins, claudins and keratins belong to other junctions or to the cytoskeleton.

items.prompt: Which of these can pass directly from one cell into a neighbour through a gap junction?
choices: Large proteins such as antibodies
Whole mitochondria, the energy organelles
Small ions and small molecules, like sugars
Cell walls, which are shared by the cells
items.explanation: Gap junction pores admit ions and molecules up to about a kilodalton, roughly the size of a small sugar. Large proteins such as antibodies cannot pass, and whole organelles and cell walls never move through a gap junction.

items.prompt: Which tissue relies on gap junctions to spread electrical signals so that it beats as one unit?
choices: Bone matrix of the skeleton
Muscle of the heart wall
Blood plasma in the vessels
Cartilage in the knee joint
items.explanation: Heart muscle cells are joined by gap junctions, so an electrical signal spreads from cell to cell and the heart contracts as one unit. Bone, blood plasma and cartilage do not depend on electrical coupling of this kind.

items.prompt: Two touching cells pass a signal through gap junctions. How does the signal travel?
choices: Ions and small molecules pass directly through the joined channels
A chemical messenger is released into the gap and binds the other cell
A hormone travels through the blood between the two cells
The two cells swap whole nuclei through the open gap
items.explanation: A gap junction joins the cytoplasm of two cells, so ions and small molecules move through the channel itself. No messenger is released into a gap, and the blood does not carry the signal between two touching cells.

items.prompt: A student says: 'Gap junctions work like a synapse, releasing messengers into a gap.' What is wrong with that?
choices: The channels join the two cytoplasms directly, so nothing is released
Gap junctions do release messengers, but only in the heart
The gap is too wide for any signal to cross from one cell
Messengers are released into the blood, which carries them over
items.explanation: A gap junction is a direct channel, so the two cells share their cytoplasm for small molecules and nothing is secreted into a gap. A synapse is the structure that releases messengers into a gap.

items.prompt: What decides whether a molecule can cross a gap junction?
choices: Its size, because the channel only admits small molecules
Whether it is a protein, since proteins pass more easily
Whether it is bound to a membrane, like a vesicle
Whether it was made in the nucleus, like mRNA
items.explanation: The channel is narrow, so size decides passage: ions and small molecules fit through and larger molecules do not, whatever their chemical type. Being a protein does not help a molecule pass.

items.prompt: Gap junctions can be closed by a change inside the cells. Which change does this?
choices: A rise in calcium inside the cells
A fall in calcium inside the cells
Gap junctions never close once they have formed
The two cells dividing at the same time
items.explanation: A rise in calcium, or a fall in pH, closes gap junction channels, which isolates a damaged cell from its neighbours. A fall in calcium does not close them, and cell division is not the trigger.

items.prompt: Heart cells are joined by gap junctions. A drug blocks those channels. What is the most likely result?
choices: Each cell's signal no longer reaches its neighbours
Each cell sends a chemical message into the gap instead
The signal reaches every cell at once, unslowed
The cells build more channels at once to compensate
items.explanation: Blocking gap junctions cuts electrical coupling, so each cell is no longer driven by its neighbours and the beat falls out of step. Cells do not switch to chemical messages when the channels are blocked.

items.prompt: A cell is injured and its calcium level rises. What do the gap junctions to its healthy neighbours most likely do?
choices: They close, which cuts the damaged cell off from its neighbours
They open wider, so healthy cells receive more calcium
They never close, so damage spreads to healthy neighbours
They release the calcium into the gap for repair
items.explanation: A rise in calcium closes gap junctions, which limits the spread of damage. They do not open wider in injury, and they do not release calcium into the gap.

items.prompt: Which structure links the cytoplasm of neighbouring plant cells across their walls?
choices: Desmosomes
Plasmodesmata
Tight junctions
Gap junctions
items.explanation: Plasmodesmata are channels through the cell walls of plants that connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells. Desmosomes, tight junctions and gap junctions are animal junctions and do not cross plant walls.

items.prompt: What runs through the centre of a plasmodesma?
choices: Nothing, since it is an empty hole in the wall
A strand of endoplasmic reticulum inside the channel
A bundle of collagen fibres running through the wall
A column of actin filaments running through the cell
items.explanation: A plasmodesma is lined by plasma membrane and holds a strand of endoplasmic reticulum, called the desmotubule, through its centre. Collagen and actin do not occur in plasmodesmata.

items.prompt: What is the main role of plasmodesmata in a plant?
choices: They connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells
They seal the walls so that water cannot leak
They build the cellulose that forms the wall
They pump calcium out through the plasma membrane
items.explanation: Plasmodesmata let neighbouring plant cells share their cytoplasm and exchange small molecules and signals. They do not seal walls, make cellulose, or pump calcium.

items.prompt: A student says: 'Plasmodesmata are just holes in the cell wall.' What is wrong with that?
choices: Each is lined by membrane and holds an ER strand inside
They do not link the cytoplasm of two cells at all
Each is a hole lined with cellulose only, so ions cannot pass
They are holes in the membrane, not in the cell wall
items.explanation: A plasmodesma is a membrane-lined channel with an ER strand through it, so the cytoplasm of the two cells is continuous. It is not an empty hole, and it is lined by plasma membrane rather than cellulose.

items.prompt: Plasmodesmata can be closed by a deposit of callose. What does this show?
choices: Plasmodesmata are regulated, so passage can be switched off
Plasmodesmata are always open, and callose only strengthens the wall
Callose makes the channels wider, so more molecules pass
Callose is a sugar that only animal cells can make
items.explanation: Callose narrows plasmodesmata and reduces what passes, which lets a plant control signalling between its cells. Callose does not widen channels, and it is made by plant cells, not animal cells.

items.prompt: Which of these can move from one plant cell to its neighbour through plasmodesmata?
choices: Sugars and small ions, such as potassium
Whole chloroplasts, such as those in leaves
Cellulose fibres, such as those in the wall
Entire nuclei, such as those with their DNA
items.explanation: Plasmodesmata let sugars and small ions pass between neighbouring cells. Chloroplasts and nuclei are far too large to move through, and cellulose is a wall material that stays in place.

items.prompt: Plasmodesmata and gap junctions both join neighbouring cells. Which difference is correct?
choices: Plasmodesmata cross a wall and contain an ER strand, which gap junctions lack
Plasmodesmata join membranes without any cytoplasm, unlike gap junctions
Gap junctions cross a cell wall, but plasmodesmata never cross any wall
They are the same structure, so the two names mean one thing
items.explanation: Both link neighbouring cells, but a plasmodesma passes through a wall and is lined by plasma membrane around an ER strand. A gap junction joins two membranes directly and has no wall to cross.

items.prompt: A small dye is put into one plant cell and spreads to every neighbour within minutes. Which route most likely carried it?
choices: Through plasmodesmata, which link the cytoplasm
Through gap junctions set into the cell walls
Through the wall itself, by soaking slowly across
Through the vacuole, which leaks into the next cell
items.explanation: Plasmodesmata let small molecules such as dyes pass from one cell's cytoplasm to its neighbour's. Gap junctions are animal structures, and the wall and vacuole do not carry dye between cells this way.

items.prompt: Callose closes the plasmodesmata in a wall. What happens to the movement of small molecules across that wall?
choices: It is reduced, so fewer molecules pass between the two cells
It is unchanged, because callose has no effect on movement
It increases, because callose widens the channel
It stops for all molecules, because the wall is sealed off
items.explanation: Callose narrows plasmodesmata, so less passes between the cells. It does not widen the channels.

items.prompt: Put these steps in the order that collagen takes from its making to its place in the matrix.
steps: Ribosomes on the rough ER make procollagen chains
Procollagen moves through the Golgi and is packed into vesicles
Vesicles fuse with the membrane and release procollagen outside
Enzymes outside the cell cut the ends off the procollagen
The collagen molecules assemble into fibrils in the matrix
items.explanation: Collagen is made as procollagen inside the cell, passed through the secretory pathway and released by exocytosis. Enzymes trim its ends outside the cell, and the trimmed molecules then assemble into fibrils.

items.prompt: Put these steps in the order that a plant cell lays down its wall after dividing.
steps: A cell plate forms between the two new nuclei
Primary wall material is laid down on each side of the plate
The cell stops growing, so its primary wall stops stretching
A secondary wall is added inside the primary wall
items.explanation: The cell plate becomes the first wall between the two daughter cells. Primary walls are laid down while the cells grow, and a secondary wall is added inside them once growth has stopped.

verification.note: solver-a's note: Step 2 (growth stops) is a late event that could be read as loosely placed, but it falls after the plate and primary wall and before the secondary wall, so the order holds.

items.prompt: Put these steps in the order that a gap junction forms between two cells.
steps: Connexin subunits assemble into a connexon in each cell's membrane
Connexons from the two cells dock across the narrow gap
The docked pair forms a pore for ions and small molecules
items.explanation: Six connexins form a connexon in each membrane. Two connexons from neighbouring cells dock across the gap to make one complete channel.

items.prompt: Tap the junction that seals the space between the two cells, so substances must pass through the cells rather than between them.
items.explanation: The tight junction is where the two membranes are pressed together by strands of claudin and occludin. The desmosome holds the cells together but leaves the gap open, and the gap junction passes small molecules from cell to cell.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “tight-junction”. a: E, hotspot “tight-junction” (agrees). b: 4, not a spot. a's note: Beaded apical strands between the cells = tight junction. Clear.

items.prompt: Tap the anchoring junction that ties into intermediate filaments, holding the cells together against pulling without sealing the space between them.
items.explanation: The desmosome is the pair of dense plaques joined across the gap by cadherins. It resists pulling but does not seal, unlike the tight junction, and it passes nothing between the cells, unlike the gap junction.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “desmosome”. a: E, hotspot “desmosome” (agrees). b: 4, not a spot. a's note: Plaque pair with rungs and intermediate filaments attached = desmosome. Clear.

items.prompt: Tap the intermediate filaments that carry a pull from the anchoring junction into the rest of the cell.
items.explanation: Keratin intermediate filaments are held by the plaque of each desmosome and run into the cytoplasm. Because they link through the desmosomes to the next cell, a pull on one cell is spread across the whole sheet.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “keratin-filaments”. a: B, hotspot “keratin-filaments” (agrees). b: 1, not a spot. a's note: Blue looping filaments in the cytoplasm = intermediate filaments.

items.prompt: Tap the junction whose connexin channels let ions pass directly from the cytoplasm of one cell into the other.
items.explanation: Each gap junction channel is two halves of connexin, one in each membrane, lined up to make a pore. The tight junction blocks the space between cells instead, and the desmosome only anchors them.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “gap-junction”. a: D, hotspot “gap-junction” (agrees). b: 3, not a spot. a's note: Gap junction is not drawn with its own label; the stacked dark bars are the only remaining junction-type feature by elimination. Moderate confidence.

items.prompt: Tap the protein fibres outside the cells that give the tissue its strength.
items.explanation: Collagen fibres lie in the extracellular matrix beneath the cells. They are made inside cells and released outward, where they give the matrix its strength, while proteoglycans in the gel around them hold water.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “collagen”. a: C, hotspot “collagen” (agrees). b: 2, not a spot. a's note: Tan wavy fibres in the extracellular matrix below the basement membrane = collagen fibres.

items.prompt: Tap the layer of cellulose fibres that resists the water pressure pushing outward from each cell.
items.explanation: The cell wall is built mainly of cellulose fibres set in a gel of other sugars. It sits outside the plasma membrane and is stiff enough to keep the cell from bursting when water builds up pressure inside.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “cell-wall”. a: D, hotspot “endoplasmic-reticulum”. b: 3, not a spot. a's note: Green cell wall outside the membrane (left diagonal). The horizontal green band at the middle could also be read as wall; the question's 'layer' wording does not separate primary from secondary wall. Moderate confidence.

items.prompt: Tap the channel that lets sugars and small signals move from the cytoplasm of one plant cell into the next.
items.explanation: The plasmodesma crosses the cell wall, and the plasma membrane lines it, so the cytoplasm of the two cells is continuous. It plays a role in plants like that of gap junctions in animals, though it is built quite differently.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “plasmodesma”. a: C, hotspot “plasmodesma” (agrees). b: 3, not a spot. a's note: Central gap region in the wall between the two cells = plasmodesma channel. Possible overlap with the membrane item at the same spot. b's note: Spot is the cytoplasm-filled channel region; the spot on the wall-gap axis could also read as the pore. Mildly ambiguous with the desmotubule spot.

items.prompt: Tap the material a plant can lay down to narrow the channel and limit what passes between the cells.
items.explanation: Callose is a sugar polymer that builds up in the wall around the channel's openings. As more is deposited, the channel narrows, which lets the plant control which signals move between its cells.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “callose”. a: E, hotspot “callose” (agrees). b: 4, not a spot. a's note: Red-brown blobs flanking the channel = callose collar.

items.prompt: Tap the membrane network that spreads through the cytoplasm and passes as a narrow tube through the channel into the next cell.
items.explanation: A narrow strand of endoplasmic reticulum runs through the middle of each plasmodesma and is continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum of both cells. The plasma membrane forms the channel's outer lining instead.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “endoplasmic-reticulum”. a: A, hotspot “cell-wall”. b: 4, not a spot. a's note: Vertical brown line through the cytoplasm of the upper cell = desmotubule (ER). The spot is near the upper cell's cytoplasm; the tube's passage through the channel is not drawn distinctly. Moderate confidence. b's note: Desmotubule spot sits on the axis in the gap between the two channel halves, not directly on the tube line; somewhat unclear.

items.prompt: Tap the membrane that bounds each cell and continues through the channel, so the two cells share one continuous surface.
items.explanation: The plasma membrane of each cell runs along the inner face of the wall and on through the channel to the next cell. This lining is why the cytoplasm of linked plant cells is continuous. The strand in the centre of the channel is endoplasmic reticulum.

verification.note: Key: hotspot “plasma-membrane”. a: D, hotspot “plasma-membrane” (agrees). b: 3, not a spot. a's note: Blue membrane outline on the lower cell's side. The item says it continues through the channel, which the spot does not clearly show; the same channel spot is used by the channel item. Moderate confidence.

artifacts.title: Junctions between two epithelial cells
artifacts.alt: Two tall epithelial cells side by side, on a thin basal lamina above a gel crossed by wavy collagen fibres. Along the gap between the cells, from top to bottom: the two membranes pinched together by rows of small beads; a pair of terracotta plaques bridged across the gap, with blue-grey filament loops running into each cell; and a stack of dark green channels spanning the gap from one cell into the other.

artifacts.title: A plasmodesma through a plant cell wall
artifacts.alt: A close-up cut through the wall between two plant cells. The wall is a tall sand-coloured band with diagonal ochre cellulose fibres and a dark middle line. A wide channel crosses the wall, lined by a blue-grey membrane that continues along both faces of the wall. A dark green tube of endoplasmic reticulum runs through the middle of the channel and branches into the cytoplasm on each side. Terracotta lumps of callose sit in the wall at both openings of the channel.
